title: The Welded
summary: Linewrought machines are repair records with legs, built to be back at work next week.
body: A chassis reaches a grade shop on a flatcar. The shop cuts away whatever seized, measures the holes that remain, and orders plate from Sarn. Nothing is put back where the Compact put it unless the old mount happens to fit. The foundries call the result Linewrought. Crews call it welded or shopwork.

A Linewrought gun is something Tessell can make: a tube, a breech, a feed chute and a shell. The racks are built the same way. They run cool enough to fire all afternoon, right up to the minute the bins run dry. Every pilot on the Line knows the sound of an empty feed striking twice.
Old Compact emitters survive on a few shop marks, carried from one opened hull to the next. No town makes one and no yard stocks a replacement.

The seams show and the plate does not match. That is useful. A fitter can reach every pump, cable and bearing without asking a dead factory for permission. A damaged machine comes home on Tuesday and may walk again by Friday, provided the shop has steel, ammunition and somebody willing to work through the night.

No two examples are identical. The mark number records trips through the shop, not a production series. A Linewrought machine is not what its first builder intended. It is what the last repair crew could afford.
